question: Outside a bar magnet, lines of magnetic flux are conventionally taken to run:

options.text: Radially outward from the centre of the magnet in all directions
From the north pole to the south pole, crossing near each pole
From the south pole to the north pole, crossing at the centre of the magnet
From the north pole to the south pole, never crossing one another

explanation: By convention flux leaves the north pole and re-enters at the south, completing its loop from south to north inside the magnet. Lines of flux never cross, since the field can have only one direction at any point.

question: Soft iron is used for the cores of relays and electromagnets because it:

options.text: Magnetises easily and loses nearly all of it when the current stops
Retains a strong magnetism indefinitely once it has been magnetised
Cannot be magnetised at all, so it does not interfere with the coil's field
Has a very high electrical resistance, so no current flows in it

explanation: Soft iron has a high permeability (it concentrates flux well) and a low retentivity (it gives that flux up when the current stops). A relay must release when de-energised — a core that stayed magnetised would hold the armature in.

question: Permanent magnets are made from materials such as hard steel or special alloys because these have:

options.text: A high retentivity and coercivity, so they keep their magnetism once magnetised
A very low electrical resistance, which allows them to carry large currents
No magnetic domains, so they cannot be demagnetised by heat or shock
A high permeability and low retentivity, so they are easily magnetised and demagnetised

explanation: Retentivity is the ability to retain magnetism; coercivity is the resistance to being demagnetised. Both are high in 'hard' magnetic materials — the opposite of what a relay core needs.

question: Reluctance in a magnetic circuit is:

options.text: The ability of a material to retain its magnetism, comparable to capacitance
Opposition to magnetic flux, the magnetic equivalent of resistance
The loss of magnetism when a material is heated above a critical temperature
The magnetising force produced by a coil, comparable to electromotive force

explanation: Flux = magnetomotive force / reluctance, the magnetic equivalent of Ohm's law. Air has a very high reluctance compared with iron, which is why even a small air gap in a relay's magnetic circuit greatly weakens its pull.

question: A magnetised piece of steel is heated above its Curie temperature. It will:

options.text: Lose its magnetism, because the alignment of its magnetic domains is destroyed
Become an electrical insulator
Reverse its polarity permanently
Become a stronger magnet, because its domains align more readily when hot

explanation: Above the Curie point thermal agitation overcomes the forces holding the domains in alignment, and the material becomes non-magnetic. Heat and mechanical shock are both ways of weakening a permanent magnet.

question: Current flows along a straight conductor. Using the right-hand grip rule, with the thumb pointing in the direction of conventional current, the fingers show:

options.text: The direction of the force on the conductor
The direction of the circular magnetic field around the conductor
The direction of electron flow in the conductor
The north pole of the field, which lies along the conductor

explanation: Any current-carrying conductor is surrounded by concentric rings of magnetic flux. Grip the conductor with the right hand, thumb along the current: the curl of the fingers gives the field direction.

question: The strength of the magnetic field produced by a coil can be increased by:

options.text: Reducing the current and removing the core to lower the reluctance
Increasing the resistance of the wire while keeping the voltage the same
More current, more turns, or a soft iron core
Spacing the turns further apart along a longer former

explanation: Magnetising force is proportional to ampere-turns. An iron core, with its far higher permeability than air, multiplies the flux produced by those ampere-turns.

question: Two long parallel conductors carry current in the same direction. The force between them is:

options.text: Zero, because their fields cancel
Attraction
Repulsion
A twisting force with no net attraction or repulsion

explanation: Between the conductors the two circular fields oppose each other and weaken, while outside they reinforce. The conductors are pushed towards the weaker field, so they attract. Currents in opposite directions repel — which is why busbars must be braced against the forces of a short-circuit current.

question: Fleming's left-hand rule is used to find:

options.text: The direction of the induced EMF in a conductor moved through a magnetic field, as in a generator
The direction of motion of a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, as in a motor
The direction of the field around a straight current-carrying conductor
The polarity of the north pole of a coil

explanation: Left hand for motors: First finger = Field, seCond finger = Current, thuMb = Motion. The right-hand rule, with the same finger assignments, gives the induced current in a generator.

question: Fleming's right-hand rule relates:

options.text: The direction of current in a coil and the position of its north pole
The phase relationship between current and voltage in an inductive circuit
The direction of the field, the current in a conductor and the resulting force on it
The direction of the magnetic field, the motion of a conductor and the resulting induced current

explanation: The right-hand (generator) rule: First finger Field, thuMb Motion of the conductor, seCond finger the induced Current. It is the counterpart of the left-hand (motor) rule.

question: The force on a conductor carrying current at right angles to a magnetic field is proportional to:

options.text: The voltage across the conductor divided by its length
Flux density, current and length of conductor in the field
The flux density and the resistance of the conductor only
The square of the current, independent of the field strength

explanation: F = BIL. Double the field, the current or the length in the field and the force doubles. If the conductor lies parallel to the field, the force is zero.

question: Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction states that the EMF induced in a circuit is proportional to:

options.text: The square of the number of turns in the circuit
The total magnetic flux linking the circuit, whether or not it is changing
The rate of change of the magnetic flux linking the circuit
The resistance of the circuit multiplied by the current in it

explanation: A steady flux induces nothing — only change does. Move a conductor faster through a field, use a stronger field, or switch a current on and off more quickly, and the induced EMF rises.

question: Lenz's law states that the direction of an induced current is such that:

options.text: It is in phase with the voltage that produced the flux
It opposes the change of flux that produced it
It always flows from north to south through the conductor
It reinforces the change of flux that produced it

explanation: Lenz's law is the conservation of energy applied to induction: the induced current always creates a field resisting its own cause. It is the origin of a motor's back-EMF and of the drag felt when a generator is loaded.

question: A conductor moves through a uniform magnetic field. The induced EMF is greatest when the conductor moves:

options.text: At 45° to the lines of flux
In any direction, since the EMF does not depend on direction
Parallel to the lines of flux
At right angles to the lines of flux

explanation: The EMF depends on the rate at which the conductor cuts flux. Moving perpendicular cuts the most lines per second; moving parallel cuts none and induces nothing. This is why a rotating generator coil produces a sine wave.

question: Self-induction in a coil is the effect by which:

options.text: The coil stores electric charge on its turns, like a capacitor
A current in one coil induces an EMF in a second, nearby coil
A changing current in a coil induces an opposing EMF in that same coil
A steady current in the coil gradually increases its own resistance

explanation: The changing field of the coil's own current cuts its own turns. The resulting back-EMF delays the rise of current at switch-on and produces a voltage spike at switch-off. Induction between two separate coils is mutual induction — the transformer principle.

question: Mutual induction between two coils is the principle on which which device operates?

options.text: The thermocouple
The capacitor
The diode
The transformer

explanation: An alternating current in the primary sets up a changing flux that links the secondary, inducing a voltage there. No changing flux — as with steady DC — means no transfer, which is why transformers do not work on DC.

question: The unit of inductance is the:

options.text: Henry
Farad
Weber
Tesla

explanation: The henry is the unit of inductance. The farad is capacitance, the weber is magnetic flux and the tesla is flux density (webers per square metre).

question: The iron cores of transformers and AC machines are made of thin laminations, insulated from one another, in order to:

options.text: Reduce eddy currents in the core and the heat they produce
Increase the core's retentivity, so that it stays magnetised
Reduce the number of turns needed in the windings
Allow the core to carry part of the load current

explanation: A changing flux induces EMFs in the core itself, driving circulating eddy currents that waste energy as heat. Thin insulated laminations break up those current paths. Hysteresis loss, the other core loss, is reduced by choosing a soft magnetic material.

question: Hysteresis loss in the core of an AC machine is energy lost:

options.text: Through eddy currents circulating within the core laminations
By friction in the bearings and windage of the rotor
As heat in the resistance of the copper windings
In reversing the core's magnetisation every cycle

explanation: Each reversal of the field must realign the core's magnetic domains, and some energy is lost as heat each time. The loss rises with frequency and is minimised by using a material with a narrow hysteresis loop, such as silicon steel.

question: When a DC supply is first switched onto an inductive coil, the current:

options.text: Rises gradually, held back by the coil's back-EMF
Jumps instantly to its final value and then stays there
Alternates at a frequency set by the inductance
Rises instantly to a peak and then decays to zero

explanation: The back-EMF of self-induction opposes the rising current, so it builds up exponentially with a time constant L/R. Once steady, only the coil's resistance limits the current. A capacitor is the opposite case: current is greatest at switch-on and decays.

question: A sensitive instrument can be protected from external magnetic fields by:

options.text: Mounting it next to a permanent magnet of opposite polarity
Wrapping it in copper braid connected to the battery positive
A soft magnetic case that diverts the flux around it
Enclosing it in a plastic case, which magnetic flux cannot pass through

explanation: Flux follows the path of least reluctance. A soft-iron or mu-metal shield gives the flux an easy route around the instrument instead of through it. Non-magnetic materials such as plastic or aluminium have essentially no effect on a steady magnetic field.

question: Residual magnetism in the field poles of a self-excited generator is important because:

options.text: It cancels the armature reaction at high loads
It limits the generator's maximum output voltage
It gives the initial flux from which the voltage builds up
It prevents the generator from being driven backwards as a motor

explanation: A self-excited generator feeds its own field from its output. With no current yet flowing, only the small leftover magnetism in the poles produces the first EMF, which then strengthens the field and so builds up. If it is lost, the field must be 'flashed' from an external supply.
